draft.title: Minimum spanning trees
card: A minimum spanning tree joins every vertex of a weighted network using the least total weight. It has no circuits. It is used for jobs such as laying cable between towns.
List the edges from smallest weight to largest. Add each edge in turn, but skip any edge that would make a circuit. Stop when every vertex is joined.
Start at any vertex. Keep adding the smallest edge that joins a new vertex to the part already built. Stop when every vertex is joined.
Edges: AB 4, AC 2, BC 3, BD 5, CD 6. Kruskal adds AC 2 and BC 3. It skips AB 4, as A, B and C would form a circuit. It adds BD 5. Total weight: 2 + 3 + 5 = 10.
draft.remember: Both methods build the cheapest way to join every vertex, and neither ever adds an edge that makes a circuit.

a.q: A network has edges PQ 3, PR 4, QR 5, RS 6 and QS 8. What is the total weight of its minimum spanning tree?
a.why: Kruskal adds PQ 3 and PR 4. It skips QR 5, as P, Q and R would form a circuit. It adds RS 6. Total: 3 + 4 + 6 = 13. The answer 12 is tempting, but 3 + 4 + 5 leaves S unconnected.
a.clue: Check each edge for a circuit before you add it.

b.q: Cable must link five towns. The costs in thousands of dollars are AB 7, AC 5, BC 6, BD 4, CD 8, CE 9 and DE 3. What is the least total cost to connect all five towns?
b.why: Kruskal adds DE 3, BD 4, AC 5 and BC 6. Every town is now joined, so the rest are not needed. Total: 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 18. Using AB 7 in place of BC 6 also joins all towns, but it costs 19, which is more.
b.clue: Take the cheapest edges first, and stop once all five towns are joined.

check.summary: No problems found. The card example (total 10) and both answers (13 and $18 000) check out with Kruskal's method, and the explanations are correct.
